title: SWR cache stores full unbounded payloads in localStorage with no per-entry size cap or eviction
description: writeSwr serializes the entire server payload (JSON.stringify) under key 'acu:swr:<path>?<params>' with no size limit and no eviction strategy. The resources endpoint is called with limit=0 (App.jsx:307, 373), so the backend returns EVERY attributed resource in the account (resources_api.py build_resources_ctx -> ctx['rows'] is the full list; effective_limit None in cost.py:144), and services/composition/data returns a dict keyed by every service, each with a full usage_types array. For an account with thousands of EC2/EBS/Lambda/S3 resources and hundreds of services x usage types, a single cached blob is multiple MB. localStorage quota is ~5MB per origin and is shared across ALL keys. Once the quota is exceeded the setItem in writeSwr throws, is swallowed by the empty catch, and is non-fatal for THAT write — but it also means no new entry can ever be written again until something is removed, silently disabling the SWR cache entirely. Old entries are never proactively evicted (only lazily removed when read AND older than STALE_MS=24h), so distinct (profile x period x region x service) combinations accumulate and permanently consume quota.
scenario: Operator points the dashboard at a large production account (5,000+ resources). The Resources page fetches /api/resources/data with limit=0; the response is ~4MB of JSON. writeSwr tries to persist it, blowing past the 5MB quota. The write is silently dropped, and every subsequent cache write across all pages also fails. The user gets zero SWR benefit and pays full CE/latency on every navigation, with no surfaced error.
suggested_fix: Cap per-entry serialized size (e.g. skip caching payloads over ~256KB), implement LRU/quota-aware eviction (on QuotaExceededError, delete oldest 'acu:swr:' keys by ts and retry), and consider not caching the full unbounded resources/composition responses at all (cache only bounded summaries). Optionally move large blobs to IndexedDB which has a far larger quota.

title: Resource and service tables render every row with no virtualization, freezing the UI at scale
description: ResourcesPage maps over (d.rows || []) to emit one <tr> per attributed resource, and the data is fetched with limit=0 (App.jsx:373) so the full account resource set is returned. There is no windowing/virtualization. For thousands of resources React must reconcile and the browser must lay out thousands of DOM rows (each with a clipboard button and cost bar), causing multi-second main-thread blocking / UI freeze on first render and on every profile/period/service change. The same pattern exists in ServicesPage (App.jsx:337-360, limit=0 at line 307 -> all services rendered, each expandable) and in ServiceComposition's 'Show all' which renders usageTypes.length rows (App.jsx:278, 295-299) — a single high-cardinality service (e.g. EC2) can have hundreds of usage types across regions.
scenario: User opens the Resources page for an account with ~8,000 attributed resources. ResourcesPage renders 8,000 table rows in one pass; the tab freezes for several seconds, and toggling the service filter (debounced) re-renders the full list again. Similarly, clicking 'Show all N usage types' on EC2 expands hundreds of rows inline, jank-locking the Services page.
suggested_fix: Virtualize the resource and service tables (react-window/react-virtual) or paginate, and request a bounded limit from the API instead of limit=0 (e.g. server-side top-N with explicit 'load more'). Cap the 'Show all usage types' expansion or virtualize it.

title: Resources fetched with limit=0 pulls the entire account resource list to the browser
description: ResourcesPage calls api.resources(profile, period, 'all', debouncedService, 0, ...) with limit=0. In cost.py:144 limit<=0 maps to effective_limit=None and resources_api.py returns the full ctx['rows'] (only sliced when limit>0). Combined with the client-side filter rebuilding on every debounced keystroke and the SWR write of the whole payload, this means the full unbounded list is transferred over the wire, JSON-parsed in the main thread, written to localStorage, and held in React state on the client. Memory and parse cost grow linearly with account size, and the parse/serialize happens synchronously on the main thread.
scenario: Account with tens of thousands of CUR-attributable line items / resources. The single /api/resources/data response is large; JSON.parse on the main thread (api.js:24) and the subsequent JSON.stringify in writeSwr both block the UI, on top of the render freeze.
suggested_fix: Pass an explicit reasonable limit (server-side top-N) from the Resources page and add a paged 'load more' control, rather than limit=0; keep the full-list path off the client entirely.

title: Clipboard write promise rejection is unhandled
description: navigator.clipboard?.writeText(r.resource_id) returns a Promise that is neither awaited nor caught. In insecure contexts (non-HTTPS, which is common for a locally-hosted dashboard on an IP address rather than localhost), clipboard?.writeText may exist but reject with a NotAllowedError, producing an unhandled promise rejection and no user feedback. There is also no success/failure indication for the copy action.
scenario: User runs the dashboard over plain HTTP on a LAN IP (not localhost) and clicks a resource ID to copy it. The write rejects, the rejection is unhandled (console error / window 'unhandledrejection'), and the user sees nothing happen with no indication of failure.
suggested_fix: Await the call inside a try/catch (or attach .catch), show a transient 'Copied'/'Copy failed' state, and fall back to a textarea+execCommand or a select-on-click affordance when the Clipboard API is unavailable.

title: Arbitrary directory creation and file write via unvalidated output_dir query param
description: The POST /api/export/run endpoint takes output_dir as a raw query parameter (line 106, default './exports') and passes it unmodified into ScheduledExportConfig(output_dir=output_dir) (line 110). run_scheduled_export then does Path(config.output_dir).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) (scheduler.py:52-53) and writes cost_report_<ts>.json/.csv/.pdf into it. There is no path validation, no confinement to a base directory, and no authentication on the route (the app installs only CECountingMiddleware; no Depends/auth on any route). An attacker who can reach the HTTP endpoint controls an absolute or traversal path, so the server will recursively create directories anywhere it has write permission and drop attacker-influenced JSON/CSV content there. Because output_dir is an absolute path it bypasses the cwd entirely. The report JSON body content is partly attacker-influenceable (account/profile string is echoed into the file as 'account'), and even pure denial-of-service via creating files under sensitive trees (e.g. inside a web root, a dotfile dir, /var/...) is achievable.
scenario: POST /api/export/run?profile=default&period=mtd&fmt=json&output_dir=/home/victim/.config/autostart writes cost_report_<timestamp>.json into the victim's autostart directory; or output_dir=/var/www/html/uploads drops a JSON file into a served web root. With fmt=csv/pdf the same applies for those extensions. On a multi-user host or any deployment where serve(host=...) is bound to a non-loopback interface, this is reachable by any network client.
suggested_fix: Reject absolute paths and any path that escapes a fixed, server-configured export base directory: resolve the candidate with Path(base, output_dir).resolve() and verify base.resolve() is a parent (os.path.commonpath / is_relative_to). Better, drop the output_dir parameter from the web API entirely (mirror /export/download which already forces a tempdir) and only allow operator-configured destinations. Also add authentication to the export routes.

title: Unvalidated profile query param selects arbitrary local AWS profile (cross-account selection / credential_process execution)
description: get_session takes profile straight from a query parameter and passes it to make_session(profile=p), which calls boto3.Session(profile_name=p) (session.py:75-83). The value is never checked against the discoverable set returned by list_profiles(). On the unauthenticated web surface, any caller can therefore name any profile present in ~/.aws/config or ~/.aws/credentials and have the dashboard query Cost Explorer / STS / resources for that account. Worse, profile selection has side effects beyond data isolation: if a named profile is configured with credential_process, boto3 will execute that external command when the session resolves credentials, and source_profile/role_arn chains will trigger AssumeRole calls — all driven purely by the untrusted profile string. The only guard is a broad try/except that silently falls back to the default session on ProfileNotFound (deps.py:110-112), which hides the difference between 'profile does not exist' and 'profile exists but you should not be able to pick it'.
scenario: A host runs the dashboard for profile 'readonly-billing' but ~/.aws/config also defines 'prod-admin' (with a credential_process that shells out to a vault helper). An attacker who can reach the endpoint requests /api/cost/summary?profile=prod-admin: boto3 resolves prod-admin, runs its credential_process, and the dashboard returns prod-admin's cost data. No allow-list check ever runs.
suggested_fix: Validate profile against the set returned by list_profiles() (plus 'default') before calling make_session; return 400 for anything not in the allow-list instead of silently falling back. Consider an explicit operator-configured allow-list of profiles the web UI may use, and add authentication so profile selection is not exposed to untrusted callers.

title: Region/account opt-in discovery and CE filter Values arrays have no cardinality guard against CE limits
description: build_ce_filter places spec.linked_accounts and spec.usage_type_substrings directly into CE Dimensions 'Values' / nested Or arrays with no size cap (lines 92-100, 133-138). Cost Explorer enforces a hard limit of 200 values per Dimensions filter and limits filter expression depth/breadth; a spec carrying hundreds of linked accounts or usage-type substrings would build an expression CE rejects with a ValidationException, and the multi-value usage_type case fans out into one Dimensions clause per substring inside an 'Or' (O(n) clauses), which can blow past CE's expression complexity limits well before 200. These fields are currently latent (no caller populates them, confirmed by grep), so impact today is nil, but the builder is the single source of truth for filter construction and provides no defense if a future tag/usage-type/linked-account selector wires user substrings in. The summary() method's len()-based reporting (lines 69, 76) similarly assumes small lists.
scenario: A future or programmatic caller constructs CostFilterSpec(linked_accounts=tuple_of_400_account_ids) or usage_type_substrings of 250 user-entered substrings (e.g. an org with hundreds of linked accounts feeding an account multi-select). build_ce_filter emits a single Dimensions Values array > 200 entries (or 250 OR clauses), and every CE call using that spec fails with a ValidationException rather than degrading gracefully.
suggested_fix: In build_ce_filter, cap or chunk Values arrays to CE's 200-entry limit (and bound the number of usage_type_substrings OR clauses), raising a clear, caught error or splitting into batched queries; document the limit on CostFilterSpec so callers wiring user input cannot silently exceed it.

title: Reflected XSS: profile/period query params raw-interpolated into inline <script> in trend-chart
description: api_trend_chart builds an HTML fragment with an f-string: data_url = f"/api/cost/trend/data?profile={profile}&period={period}" and then embeds it directly inside an inline <script> as fetch("{data_url}"). Both `profile` and `period` are attacker-controlled Query params with NO validation, escaping, or allow-listing anywhere in the request path (period_to_window/deps.py just .get(period, current_month) and never rejects unknown values). Because the value lands inside a JS string literal in an inline <script>, an attacker can break out of the string and the script context. Returned via HTMLResponse with no escaping. The route is reachable directly by URL (GET /api/cost/trend-chart) and via hx-get from pages, so a crafted link is a classic reflected-XSS delivery vector against any dashboard operator who clicks it; the dashboard runs against live AWS credentials, so script execution can pivot to triggering money-spending CE/describe calls or exfiltrating page contents (account IDs, ARNs, cost data).
scenario: Operator opens /api/cost/trend-chart?profile=%22)%3B%7Dalert(document.domain)%3B(()%3D%3E%7Bfetch(%22&period=3m (i.e. profile = "");}alert(document.domain);(()=>{fetch("). The injected text closes the fetch() string and statement, runs alert/arbitrary JS, then re-opens a call so the rest of the template still parses. Same applies to period. Even simpler: profile=" closes the inline script tag and injects an HTML element with an event handler.
suggested_fix: Do not interpolate user input into inline script/HTML. Either (a) JSON-encode and additionally escape script-breaking sequences, e.g. build the URL with urllib.parse.urlencode({"profile": profile, "period": period}) and inject via a data-* attribute on the canvas that charts.js reads, or (b) validate profile against the known profile_choices list and period against an explicit allow-list (mtd/last_month/30d/3m/...) and 400 on anything else, plus HTML-escape before embedding. Best: emit the URL into a data attribute and have static JS read it, never building <script> bodies from request input.

title: Inline-script chart fragment uses json.dumps for labels, which does not escape </script> or angle brackets
description: api_cost_services with chart=1 returns HTMLResponse containing <script>buildServiceChart('service-chart',{json.dumps(labels)},{json.dumps(values)});</script>. json.dumps is NOT an HTML/script-safe encoder: it leaves </script>, <, > and U+2028/U+2029 intact (verified: json.dumps(['</script>...']) emits the literal </script>). `labels` are service names sliced from ctx['services'] (s['name'][:24]). If any label contains the substring </script> (or an injected </script><...> via a downstream data source such as CUR-derived/usage-type-derived names that can carry arbitrary strings), the browser closes the inline <script> early and renders the remainder as HTML, enabling stored/reflected XSS. The 24-char slice does not prevent </script> (9 chars) plus a short tag from fitting.
scenario: A CUR line item or grouped key produces a service label containing ''. When the chart fragment is requested (GET /api/cost/services?chart=1), json.dumps emits the closing tag verbatim inside the inline script, the script terminates, and the injected img tag's onerror fires in the operator's session.
suggested_fix: Escape the JSON for an HTML script context before embedding: replace '<' with '<', '>' with '>', '&' with '&', and U+2028/U+2029, e.g. json.dumps(...).replace('<','\\u003c').replace('>','\\u003e').replace('&','\\u0026'). Better, render the chart via a data island (<script type="application/json">) parsed by static JS, or pass data through an endpoint fetched by charts.js rather than inlining.

title: friendly_error leaks raw AWS exception text (ARNs, account IDs, internal detail) to clients
description: friendly_error falls through to `return f"AWS error: {msg[:160]}"`, echoing the first 160 chars of the raw exception string straight into HTTP responses (rendered in partials/audit_findings, cost_cards, resource_table, and JSON ...//data endpoints). boto3/botocore ClientError messages routinely embed the caller ARN, 12-digit account ID, resource ARNs, principal names, and operation/endpoint detail (e.g. 'User: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/bob is not authorized to perform ce:GetCostAndUsage on resource ...'). The AccessDenied branch only triggers when the literal 'AccessDenied'/'not authorized' appears; many authorization and validation errors (ValidationException, throttling, DataUnavailable with request IDs) fall through to the raw echo. This is information disclosure on an unauthenticated app and the leaked strings are then placed into HTML without the operator controlling them.
scenario: CE call fails with a botocore ValidationException or an AccessDenied phrased differently than the matched literals; the raw message containing the account ID and full ARN is returned in ctx['error'] and rendered to the page / returned as JSON, exposing internal identifiers to anyone who can reach the endpoint (no auth required).
suggested_fix: Return only sanitized, category-level messages; log the full exception server-side (it is already imported as logging elsewhere). Map known botocore error codes to generic strings and use a fixed fallback like 'AWS error — see server logs' instead of echoing msg[:160]. Never interpolate the raw message into responses.

title: No authentication/authorization on any route; all cost/resource/audit endpoints spend AWS money unauthenticated
description: The FastAPI app registers all routers (pages, cost, resources_api, audit_api, export_api) with no auth dependency, no Security/Depends gate, and no global auth middleware (only CECountingMiddleware, which just counts). Every endpoint — /api/cost/*, /api/resources/*, /api/audit/summary, /api/export/run — calls Cost Explorer (billed per request + per UsageRecord, per middleware.py estimated_usd) and broad describe/audit APIs using the server's local AWS credentials. Any party that can reach the bound socket can trigger unbounded, cost-incurring AWS API fan-out (e.g. /api/resources across ALL_REGIONS, /api/audit across all regions, deep CE pagination) with arbitrary profile/period/region. Combined with the XSS findings, a crafted link executes in an operator's browser and can drive these money-spending calls. There is no rate limit either.
scenario:
App is started with serve() and (intentionally or via misconfiguration/SSRF/exposed port beyond 127.0.0.1) reachable by another host/user. The attacker loops GET /api/resources/data?profile=

®ion=all and GET /api/audit/summary/data, each fanning out describe/CE calls across every opted-in region and accumulating CE charges, with zero authentication to stop them.
suggested_fix: Add an authentication gate (shared-secret token via Depends/Security, or bind strictly to loopback and document it) on at least all routers that construct AWS sessions and call AWS. Add rate limiting and consider an allow-list of profiles. Even for a localhost tool, require a token to mitigate DNS-rebinding/CSRF-driven money spend.

title: Cross-site request can trigger state/cost-affecting POSTs (cache clear, export run) — no CSRF protection
description: POST routes exist (/api/cache/clear and /api/export/run in export_api, the former invoked from base.html via hx-post) and the app installs no CSRF protection and no SameSite/Origin checks. Because there is also no authentication and CORS is default (no CORSMiddleware, so simple cross-origin form/HTMX POSTs from an attacker page are not blocked at the network layer for same-site/localhost contexts), a malicious page the operator visits can issue a cross-site POST to /api/export/run?profile=...&period=... which spins up a full report build (CE matrix + trend + resource attribution across regions, money-spending) and to /api/cache/clear which wipes the warm cache forcing expensive cold refetches. DNS-rebinding makes this exploitable even for a 127.0.0.1-bound server.
scenario: Operator with the dashboard running on localhost browses to an attacker-controlled page that auto-submits a form/fetch POST to http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/export/run?profile=prod&period=3m. The server executes the export pipeline (multiple CE calls + cross-region resource attribution) on the victim's credentials, incurring cost, with no token or Origin check rejecting the request.
suggested_fix: Require an auth token on all POST routes and verify Origin/Referer (or a CSRF token) against an allow-list. Bind to loopback and add a per-session anti-CSRF token for state/cost-changing POSTs. Do not rely on browser CORS for protection — simple POSTs are not preflighted.

title: Full resource/service contexts (entire row sets) serialized to JSON / re-sorted per request — unbounded memory and O(n log n) per call for huge accounts
description: build_resources_ctx materializes ctx['rows'] as a full list of every attributed resource (one dict per EC2 instance / Lambda fn / S3 bucket / EBS vol / CUR line item) for the whole account, then api_resources_data / api_resources_top sort and JSONResponse the entire structure. For an account with tens of thousands of resources this means: (1) the full list and its normalized dict copies live in memory; (2) the whole blob is stored in the SQLite cache via cache_set (large serialized payload, copied on every dict(cached)); (3) /data and /top re-sort the entire list (sorted over all rows) and serialize all of it on each request even when limit is small; (4) services_summary aggregation iterates all rows building two dicts. There is no server-side cap on returned rows when limit<=0 in /data and the HTML route, so a single request can emit a multi-megabyte JSON/HTML response. dict(cached) in the SWR path shallow-copies the top-level dict but the giant 'rows' list is shared/re-sorted, and copy/serialize cost scales with total resource count regardless of the limit the caller wants.
scenario: Profile points at a large account (e.g. 50k EC2/EBS/Lambda/S3 objects or a fat CUR export). GET /api/resources/data?limit=0 (or the HTML /api/resources with no limit) builds and serializes the entire row set; concurrent dashboard widgets (/top, /services) each shallow-copy and re-sort all rows. Memory spikes and response sizes balloon into the MBs, and the SQLite cache stores the entire blob, slowing every subsequent get/copy.
suggested_fix: Cap rows server-side (enforce a sane max even when limit<=0) and store a pre-sorted, pre-truncated 'top N' plus aggregate totals in the cache rather than the full row list. Compute services_summary once and cache it separately. For full exports, stream/paginate instead of returning one JSON blob, and avoid re-sorting the entire list on every /top request (sort once at build time).

title: Nested ThreadPoolExecutors multiply into 70+ concurrent threads, and each thread opens many boto3 clients/connections
description: The outer pool is sized min(16, max(len(regions)*2,4)) — up to 16 workers. Six services (RDS, EIP, ELB, Lambda, S3, DynamoDB) each run via _fanout_regions, and EACH _fanout_regions opens its OWN inner ThreadPoolExecutor of min(12, len(regions)) workers (line 114). With ~20 opted-in regions and all six fan-out jobs running concurrently in the outer pool, that is up to 6 inner pools * 12 = 72 region-worker threads alive simultaneously, plus the EC2 job and the sequential EBS job, plus the outer pool threads themselves. Every region worker then creates fresh boto3 clients (rds/ec2/elb/lambda/s3/dynamodb + cloudwatch), each holding its own connection pool. Thread and socket count explodes, and because the outer pool only has 16 slots, the six fan-out submissions can be serialized while still each spawning 12 inner threads, giving bursty 72-thread spikes.
scenario: A management/payer-style account with ~20 opted-in regions runs the default region='all' enumerate_all (the path cost_store.py uses). All six per-region services plus EC2 and EBS launch at once; the process briefly holds 70-90 live threads and hundreds of open HTTPS connections, risking thread-pool starvation, file-descriptor exhaustion, and AWS API throttling storms.
suggested_fix: Use a single shared bounded executor for all (service, region) work units instead of nesting a new ThreadPoolExecutor per service. Build a flat list of (fn, session, region, extra) tasks and submit them all to one pool with a fixed cap (e.g. 16-24). This bounds total concurrency regardless of region/service count.

title: EC2 per-region CE query has no REGION filter, so the same account-wide EC2 cost is counted once per region
description: attribute_ec2_account loops over every region and calls _attribute_from_usage_type once per region. Inside, the CE GetCostAndUsage filter (lines 72-79) contains only the base spec filter plus a SERVICE=EC2-Compute dimension — there is NO REGION dimension. The CE client is the single us-east-1 raw client passed down from runner.py (ce_raw), so each per-region call returns the SAME global EC2 cost-by-usage-type. The code then enumerates instances only in that region and allocates the global CE cost across them. Across N regions this attributes roughly N times the true EC2 spend in aggregate (each region's instances get a slice of the full account total). The USAGE_TYPE keys do carry a region prefix that is stripped (line 102), confirming the response is account-wide, not region-scoped.
scenario: An account running EC2 in 3 regions: real EC2 cost is $300. enumerate_all(region='all') calls _attribute_from_usage_type 3 times, each seeing the full $300 split by usage type, and each splitting that $300 across only that region's running instances. Summed EC2 attributed cost approaches $900 (3x), and since EC2 has no later CE-total rescaling step (only EBS/EIP, RDS/ELB are rescaled), the inflated total flows straight to the dashboard.
suggested_fix: Add a REGION dimension to the CE filter keyed to the loop's region (And the SERVICE filter with {Dimensions:{Key:'REGION',Values:[region]}}), or query CE once with GroupBy [USAGE_TYPE, REGION] and partition results by region before splitting across that region's instances.

title: EC2 USAGE_TYPE parser drops us-east-1 (un-prefixed) usage types entirely
description: raw.split('-', 1)[1] strips the regional prefix (e.g. 'APS3-BoxUsage:t3.micro' -> 'BoxUsage:t3.micro'). But us-east-1 usage types have NO regional prefix in CE — they appear as bare 'BoxUsage:t3.micro'. For those, raw contains no '-' before 'BoxUsage', so the code falls into the `else: raw` branch giving rest='BoxUsage:t3.micro'... actually for 'BoxUsage:m5.large' there is no '-', so rest=raw='BoxUsage:m5.large' and it DOES match. However many us-east-1 usage types do contain a hyphen inside the instance family or modifier (e.g. 'BoxUsage:t3.micro' has none, but 'EBSOptimized:...' and dedicated/host types like 'DedicatedUsage:...' aside, types like 'BoxUsage:c5d.large' are fine). The real breakage: when the usage type itself begins differently or the first hyphen lands inside the descriptor, the split mis-parses. More importantly, any us-east-1 BoxUsage with a hyphen-less name that the heuristic strips will mis-key. The split('-',1) approach is fragile and silently produces 'continue' (line 110) for unmatched buckets, dropping that EC2 cost from attribution.
scenario: Account whose EC2 runs in us-east-1 only. CE returns 'BoxUsage:t3.large' (no prefix). split('-',1) finds no hyphen so rest=raw and it matches — but 'SpotUsage:...' un-prefixed likewise. For regions whose code maps differently or for usage types whose first token contains a hyphen, the bucket silently hits `continue` and that EC2 spend never appears in any per-instance row, under-reporting EC2.
suggested_fix: Do not rely on positional hyphen splitting. Instead search for the known markers directly: find 'BoxUsage:', 'SpotUsage:', 'HeavyUsage:' anywhere in the raw key (rfind/`in`) and slice from there, so both prefixed and un-prefixed usage types parse correctly and nothing is silently dropped.

title: CE-total rescaling factor can divide by a near-zero raw_sum, massively inflating per-resource cost
description: EBS/EIP rescaling computes factor = other_pool / raw_sum and RDS/ELB compute factor = ce_tot / raw_sum, guarded only by `raw_sum > 0`. raw_sum is the sum of locally-priced resource costs. If pricing fell back to 0 for most resources (unknown instance/volume types -> FALLBACK_RATES lookup returns 0.0, e.g. an EC2/EBS type not in the table, or RDS where rds_instance_rate returns 0.0 for unknown classes), raw_sum can be a tiny positive number while other_pool/ce_tot is large. factor becomes enormous and is multiplied onto every row. A single cheap-but-nonzero resource absorbs the entire service pool, and resources priced at 0 get nothing — gross misattribution.
scenario: Account with 500 EBS volumes of a type missing from FALLBACK_RATES so most price at $0, but one gp3 volume prices at $0.01. EC2-Other pool from CE is $2,000. raw_sum=$0.01, factor=200000. That one volume is shown as $2,000 while the other 499 show $0 — the dashboard tells the user a single tiny volume costs the entire EC2-Other bill.
suggested_fix: Clamp the factor (e.g. cap at some sane multiple, or skip rescaling when raw_sum is below a threshold relative to the pool), and/or distribute residual pool across zero-cost resources by size/hours instead of letting one nonzero resource absorb it. Surface the variance_from_ground_truth as a drift warning rather than silently rescaling.

title: ELB attribution issues describe_target_health once per target group (N+1), unbounded under many TGs
description: For every target group in the region the code calls elbv2.describe_target_health(TargetGroupArn=...) individually inside the paginator loop. There is no batching (the API has none) and no cap. With hundreds or thousands of target groups in a busy region this is a serial N+1 fan of API calls on a single thread, multiplied across every region by the runner fan-out. describe_target_health is also rate-limited; under fan-out this will trigger throttling (ClientError) which is caught broadly at line 49 and abandons ALL healthy-target data for the region, silently disabling the 'no healthy targets' waste flag.
scenario: Region with 2,000 target groups across many ALBs. attribute_elb makes 2,000 sequential describe_target_health calls for that region alone; with ~20 regions fanned out concurrently this is tens of thousands of throttle-prone calls. The first ThrottlingException trips the except at line 49, wiping healthy_by_lb and disabling waste detection for the whole region.
suggested_fix: Only resolve target health for LBs that matter (e.g. top-cost or on demand), batch/limit the number of TGs inspected per region, add retry/backoff, and catch throttling per-call rather than abandoning the whole region's data.

title: S3 attribution makes per-bucket get_bucket_location + get_bucket_tagging + CloudWatch calls for ALL buckets in EVERY region
description: list_buckets is global, so attribute_s3 is invoked once per region by the fan-out, and each invocation calls get_bucket_location for EVERY bucket in the account (line 39) to filter to the current region, then for the surviving buckets calls get_metric_statistics (line 59) and get_bucket_tagging (line 96). With B buckets and R regions this is O(B*R) get_bucket_location calls plus O(B) CloudWatch + tagging calls per region. For an account with thousands of buckets across 20 regions this is tens of thousands of S3/CloudWatch API calls, heavily throttle-prone and slow, all under the concurrent region fan-out. get_bucket_location/get_bucket_tagging throttling is silently swallowed (continue/pass), so buckets get dropped or untagged inconsistently.
scenario: Account with 5,000 S3 buckets and 20 opted-in regions. The S3 fan-out runs attribute_s3 20 times; each calls get_bucket_location 5,000 times = 100,000 location calls, plus CloudWatch per in-region bucket. This dominates runtime and trips S3 request throttling, causing buckets to be silently dropped from attribution.
suggested_fix: Call list_buckets once globally, resolve each bucket's region once (cache location), and group buckets by region before dispatching, rather than re-listing and re-locating all buckets in every region worker. Bound the CloudWatch fan-out (as already done for Lambda/DynamoDB) and consider GetMetricData batching.

title: EBS attribution runs strictly sequentially across all regions on a single thread
description: Unlike RDS/EIP/ELB/Lambda/S3/DynamoDB which fan out per region, EBS uses _ebs_all_regions which is a plain `for reg in regions` loop. Within each region it first calls live_instance_names (a full describe_instances pagination over every non-terminated instance) and then attribute_ebs (a full describe_volumes pagination). All of this is serial across regions inside one outer-pool worker. For accounts with thousands of volumes/instances across 20 regions, EBS becomes the long-tail that gates total latency while every other service finishes.
scenario: Account with 10,000 EBS volumes and 5,000 instances spread over 20 regions. Every other service completes in parallel, but EBS walks region-by-region: 20 sequential describe_instances + describe_volumes pagination passes, taking minutes while holding the result, making the whole enumerate_all call wall-clock-bound on EBS alone.
suggested_fix: Fan EBS out per region like the other services (it already receives per-region names via live_instance_names). Pair the instance-name lookup and volume enumeration into one per-region task submitted to the shared pool.

title: live_instance_names is called for EBS and then describe_instances is paginated AGAIN for EC2 — duplicate full instance scans
description: _attribute_from_usage_type (EC2 path) paginates describe_instances over the entire region to build inst_by_key, and live_instance_names (EBS path) independently paginates describe_instances over the same region again to build the id->name map. Both run for the same regions in the same enumerate_all call. For large fleets this doubles the describe_instances work and API calls per region, compounding under the region fan-out and adding throttling pressure.
scenario: Region with 8,000 EC2 instances. EC2 attribution paginates all 8,000 instances; EBS attribution (live_instance_names) paginates the same 8,000 again. Across 20 regions that is 40 full instance scans where 20 would suffice, doubling DescribeInstances throttle exposure.
suggested_fix: Build the instance list once per region (id->name plus the type/lifecycle/hours metadata) and share it between the EC2 usage-type attribution and the EBS attached-name lookup.

title: All resources for the entire account are accumulated into one fully-buffered list, sorted, and returned/serialized
description: buckets holds every AttributedResource (one dataclass per EC2 instance, EBS volume, RDS, ELB, EIP, Lambda fn, S3 bucket, DynamoDB table across all regions), then flat extends them all into one list (216-219), sorts it (220), and returns it. Callers (cost_store / resources_api) then serialize this whole list. There is no pagination, no top-N truncation, and to_dict embeds full tags + attributes dicts per row. For an account with hundreds of thousands of resources this is a multi-hundred-MB in-memory blob that is then JSON-serialized in one shot, risking OOM and very large HTTP/cache payloads.
scenario: Account with 50,000 EBS volumes + 20,000 Lambda functions + 10,000 instances. enumerate_all builds an ~80,000-element list of dataclasses each carrying tag/attribute dicts, sorts it, and resources_api serializes the entire thing into a single JSON response and/or cache blob — hundreds of MB held and transmitted at once.
suggested_fix: Apply server-side top-N / pagination and aggregate the long tail into a synthetic 'other resources' row, or stream results. Avoid materializing and serializing the full per-resource list for very large accounts.

title: EIP cost is computed from window length, not actual association state over the window — and idle rate applied to attached EIPs
description: Every Elastic IP is charged window_hours * eip_idle_rate regardless of whether it was attached the whole time. cost is computed identically for associated and unassociated addresses (line 37 uses idle_rate for all). Since Feb 2024 AWS charges $0.005/hr for ALL public IPv4 (attached or not), but the rate constant is named eip_idle_rate and the same flat value is applied without accounting for partial-window allocation (no clamp to allocation time) or for the EIP being newly allocated mid-window. This both over-charges EIPs that existed only part of the window and is then fed into the EC2-Other rescaling pool, perturbing the EBS/EIP factor.
scenario: An EIP allocated yesterday is charged for the full 30-day window (720h * $0.005 = $3.60) instead of ~24h. Its inflated cost enters raw_sum for the EC2-Other rescaling at runner.py line 168, skewing the factor and misattributing the EBS/EIP pool.
suggested_fix: Clamp EIP billable hours to the time the address actually existed/was billable within the window (AWS does not expose allocation time directly, but at minimum cap at window_hours only when known-present; otherwise treat as best-effort and flag drift). Keep attached vs idle semantics explicit.

title: DynamoDB describe_table called serially for every table (N+1) with no cap, blocking on large table counts
description: After list_tables, the code calls ddb.describe_table once per table name in a serial loop with no upper bound, then (if should_collect_cw) issues two get_metric_statistics calls per table, then list_tags_of_resource per table. For accounts with thousands of DynamoDB tables in a region this is thousands of serial describe_table calls plus per-table CloudWatch and tagging calls. The should_collect_cw guard (len(descs) <= 50) bounds CloudWatch fan-out but NOT the describe_table or list_tags_of_resource loops, which always run for every table.
scenario: Region with 3,000 DynamoDB tables. attribute_dynamodb issues 3,000 serial describe_table calls plus 3,000 list_tags_of_resource calls (line 103 runs unconditionally) regardless of the CW guard, multiplied across the region fan-out, slow and throttle-prone.
suggested_fix: Cap the number of tables described (e.g. top by size or first N), and skip per-table list_tags_of_resource for zero-cost tables and in fast mode (as Lambda does). Bound describe_table the same way CloudWatch is bounded.

title: S3 row name lookup references tag_resp which may be unbound when get_bucket_tagging raised
description: tag_resp is assigned only inside the try block (line 96). If get_bucket_tagging raises ClientError, the except sets tags but leaves tag_resp unbound from a prior iteration. Line 104 reads `tag_name(tag_resp if tags else None, ...) if tags else name`. Because tags would be {} (falsy) when the exception fired in THIS iteration, the outer `if tags else name` selects `name`, so tag_resp is not evaluated — safe in that case. But if a PRIOR bucket succeeded (binding tag_resp) and the CURRENT bucket's tagging also succeeds with a non-empty TagSet, tags is truthy and tag_resp is the current value — fine. The latent hazard is that tag_resp leaks across loop iterations and the name logic is coupled to a name resolved from S3 tag dicts via tag_name which expects list-of-{Key,Value} dicts, while tags_to_dict already consumed them. The construct is fragile and one refactor away from a NameError / wrong-bucket name.
scenario: Refactor that makes get_bucket_tagging return a non-empty TagSet for a bucket while the `tags` truthiness check changes would surface a stale tag_resp from the previous bucket, naming the current bucket after the previous one's Name tag.
suggested_fix: Initialize tag_resp=[] before the try and derive the display name directly from the already-built tags dict (tags.get('Name', name)) instead of re-parsing tag_resp, mirroring the Lambda/DynamoDB pattern.

title: Broad bare-Exception swallowing in fan-out hides throttling and returns partial/zero attribution silently
description: _fanout_regions catches all exceptions per region (line 122) and only logs a warning, and the outer job-result collection (line 160) sets buckets[label]=[] on any failure. Under heavy fan-out, the most likely exception is API throttling (ClientError ThrottlingException). When a region or an entire service throttles, its resources are silently dropped to empty and the corresponding CE pool either goes unrescaled (EC2/Lambda/S3/DDB take CE total but lose per-resource rows) or, for RDS/ELB, the rescaling is skipped (raw_sum empty) — so the dashboard under-reports without any user-visible drift indicator beyond a log line.
scenario: 20-region account where DescribeDBInstances throttles in 5 regions during fan-out. Those regions' RDS rows are dropped to []; total RDS attributed cost is understated and the RDS CE-total rescaling (which would have corrected the sum) operates on a partial raw_sum, so per-instance costs are inflated for the surviving regions while the missing regions show nothing.
suggested_fix: Add retry/backoff (botocore adaptive retries) before giving up, and propagate a per-service 'partial/incomplete' flag into the result so the UI can warn that attribution is incomplete rather than presenting understated numbers as authoritative.

title: Month-end forecast drops the remainder of today (forecast window starts tomorrow midnight)
description: remainder_of_current_month() starts the forecast window at tomorrow 00:00 UTC (start = (now + 1 day).replace(hour=0...)). In cost.py _build_summary_ctx the month-end projection is computed as ctx['forecast'] = mtd_amount + forecast_cv.amount_usd, where mtd_amount = current_month().total() covers [1st 00:00, now]. The interval [now, tomorrow 00:00 UTC] (the rest of today) is covered by NEITHER the MTD actual NOR the forecast window. The projected month total therefore systematically omits the cost of the current partial day, under-projecting end-of-month spend.
scenario: Account spending ~$10k/day. User loads the summary at 02:00 UTC. MTD actual covers up to 02:00; forecast covers tomorrow-midnight onward. ~22 hours of today's spend (~$9k) is in the projected-month figure's blind spot, so the forecast card reads ~$9k low versus what the AWS console projects. The gap is largest early in the UTC day.
suggested_fix: Start the forecast window at the current MTD window's end (now, the same instant MTD stops) rather than at tomorrow midnight, e.g. start = now (or the next CE-allowed boundary) so [MTD end, forecast start] has no gap; or add the partial-day actual explicitly. Ensure CE's Start>=today constraint is still satisfied.

title: Previous-period comparison uses a calendar month against a non-month window (length mismatch)
description: prev_window = period_to_window('last_month') if period in ('mtd','3m','30d') else period_to_window('3m'). For period='30d' the current window is last_n_days(30) (a rolling 30-day window via deps.period_to_window), but the previous window is last_month() — a full calendar month (28-31 days, fixed [1st,1st)). change_pct = (total - prev)/prev*100 then compares a trailing-30-day sum against a calendar-month sum of different length and different alignment. For period='3m' it is worse: the current window is last_n_days(90) (90 days) compared against last_month() (~30 days), so change_pct compares ~90 days of spend to ~30 days — roughly a 3x inflation that looks like a +200% spike.
scenario: User selects the '3m' period. Current window = 90 days (~$30k), prev = last calendar month (~$10k). change_pct = (30000-10000)/10000*100 = +200%, displayed as a massive cost increase that is purely an artifact of comparing windows of different length.
suggested_fix: Derive the previous window from the SAME window length/granularity as the current one (e.g., for an N-day rolling window, prev = the immediately preceding N-day window; for mtd, prev = same-day-of-month range of prior month or full last month with an explicit 'partial vs full' note). Make period_to_window return the length so the comparison window can mirror it.

title: Services-page prev-period map mismatched for 3m and uses calendar month for 30d
description: prev_window = period_to_window('last_month') if period in ('mtd','30d') else period_to_window('3m'). Note 'mtd' and '30d' both map prev to last_month() (calendar month), while every other period (including '3m'=90 days, '6m', '12m') maps prev to period_to_window('3m')=last_n_days(90). The per-service change_pct in service_rows_from_groups (cost-prev)/prev then compares: (a) for 30d, a rolling 30-day cost against a calendar-month cost (length/alignment mismatch); (b) for 3m, a 90-day window against a 90-day window that is the SAME rolling window (prev == current for 3m → every change_pct ≈ 0%); (c) for 6m/12m, a months-long current window against only 90 days of 'prev'. All three yield misleading per-service deltas.
scenario: User opens Services for period='3m'. current window and prev_window are both last_n_days(90) → identical → prev_map equals current totals → every service shows ~0% change even when spend doubled month over month. For period='6m', prev is only 90 days vs a 6-month current window, so deltas are nonsensical.
suggested_fix: Compute prev_window as the immediately-preceding window of the same length as the selected period, consistently for all periods, instead of the ad hoc mapping. Share one helper with _build_summary_ctx.

title: get_trend assigns the whole-window provenance to every per-bucket point (dead `if False` branch)
description: bucket_window is computed with a `... if False else window` expression that always evaluates to the caller's full window. Every TimeSeriesPoint's CostValue.provenance therefore reports the entire trend window (e.g. 2025-01-01 → 2025-04-01) as the window for a single daily/monthly bucket, while period_start/period_end carry the true bucket. provenance.label() (shown on hover / in PDFs) will state the wrong time range for each point, violating the module's stated accuracy invariant that a number always answers 'where did this come from?'. The numeric amount is correct; only the provenance metadata is wrong.
scenario: User hovers a single day's bar in the 3-month daily trend. The provenance tooltip reads 'UnblendedCost · 2025-03-01 → 2025-06-01 · UTC' for a bar that actually represents only 2025-04-15, contradicting the displayed date.
suggested_fix: Build a real per-bucket TimeWindow from period['TimePeriod'] Start/End (parsed as UTC midnights) and pass that to _build_provenance, removing the `if False` dead code.

title: Forecast metric not validated/mapped for UsageQuantity and NormalizedUsageAmounts
description: The forecast_metric translation dict only maps the five cost metrics. If a caller passes CostMetric.USAGE_QUANTITY or NORMALIZED_USAGE, .get(metric.value, metric.value) falls through to the CamelCase value ('UsageQuantity'), which is not a valid get_cost_forecast Metric enum (CE expects e.g. USAGE_QUANTITY). The call raises, is swallowed by the broad except, logged as a warning, and get_forecast returns None — the forecast silently disappears with no surfaced reason. Today callers only pass cost metrics, so this is latent, but the silent-None behavior masks a real programming error.
scenario: A future caller adds a usage-quantity forecast card and passes CostMetric.USAGE_QUANTITY. The forecast endpoint rejects the metric, the exception is caught generically, and the UI shows no forecast and no error, leaving the metric mapping bug invisible.
suggested_fix: Map all CostMetric members (including USAGE_QUANTITY→'USAGE_QUANTITY', NORMALIZED_USAGE→'NORMALIZED_USAGE_AMOUNT') or raise a clear ValueError for unsupported forecast metrics instead of passing an invalid value through.

title: EC2 merge set in service_groups.py does not match the EC2 raw names used in the composition route
description: EC2_MERGE_SOURCES = {'Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud - Compute', 'EC2 - Other'}. CE's SERVICE dimension actually returns 'EC2 - Other' in some accounts but in many it returns the full 'Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud - Compute' for compute and a separate value. More importantly the merge target name here is 'Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud', and the route's _EC2_RAW_NAMES (cost.py line 236-239) uses the SAME two strings — so they agree with each other — but neither set includes other common CE EC2 split values such as 'Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud' (already-merged) appearing alongside 'EC2 - Other', nor the data-transfer split. The real risk: merge_ec2_service_groups only collapses exactly these two literal strings; if CE returns 'Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud - Compute' AND the account also has e.g. 'Amazon EC2 - Other' (note 'Amazon' prefix variation seen across CE versions), the 'EC2 - Other' literal won't match and that spend stays as a separate row, so the merged EC2 total under-reports versus the console's single EC2 line.
scenario: An account where CE labels the second EC2 row 'Amazon EC2 - Other' instead of 'EC2 - Other'. merge_ec2_service_groups leaves it unmerged, so the dashboard shows two EC2-related rows and the 'Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud' row is lower than the console's EC2 line by the EC2-Other amount.
suggested_fix: Match EC2 sub-services by prefix/substring (e.g. names containing 'Elastic Compute Cloud' or starting with 'EC2'/'Amazon EC2') rather than an exact two-element frozenset, and keep service_groups.py and cost.py sharing one canonical merge definition.

title: Composition route drops negative line items, diverging the composition total from the service total
description: In _build_services_composition_ctx, `if amount <= 0: continue` skips every SERVICE×USAGE_TYPE group with non-positive cost. Even under pre_credit_gross() (which excludes Credit/Refund/Upfront) CE can still return negative UnblendedCost line items for SavingsPlan/RI adjustments, EDP discounts, or usage-type-level negative true-ups. Dropping them makes the per-service composition 'total' (sum(buckets.values()), line 303) larger than the service's true net spend shown on the Services page (service_rows_from_groups sums all groups including negatives). The composition bars and the headline service cost will not reconcile.
scenario: A service with a -$2,000 SavingsPlanNegation usage type and +$10,000 of compute. The Services page shows $8,000 for the service; the composition view shows $10,000 total (compute bucket), a $2,000 discrepancy the user cannot explain.
suggested_fix: Do not filter out negative amounts; accumulate them into their bucket so composition totals reconcile with the service total. If hiding tiny rows in the UI is desired, filter on display only (e.g. abs(cost) below a threshold) and keep the bucket math complete.

title: Per-service usage_type list is unbounded — huge serialized JSON for high-cardinality services
description: ctx['services'] builds, for every service, a fully sorted usage_types list containing one entry per distinct USAGE_TYPE accumulated across all regions in usage_by_svc. CE USAGE_TYPE cardinality is regional (e.g. 'APN1-BoxUsage:m5.large', 'USE1-BoxUsage:m5.large', ...). For an account spanning dozens of regions and hundreds of instance/usage types, a single service (EC2) can have thousands of usage types. All of them are sorted and serialized into the cached JSON and returned on every /services/composition/data hit. There is no limit parameter and the result is cached (cache_set), so the blob is held in SQLite and re-deserialized each request.
scenario: Management account with 1000+ EC2 instances across 20 regions. EC2 alone yields ~5,000 USAGE_TYPE rows; the composition JSON for one period is multiple MB, the per-service sort is O(n log n) on thousands of items per service, and the cached blob bloats the SQLite cache. The composition endpoint becomes the slowest/heaviest route.
suggested_fix: Cap usage_types per service (e.g. top 25 by cost with an aggregated 'other' remainder) before serialization, or expose a limit query param. Keep bucket totals exact while truncating the detail list.

title: CostStore matrix cache stores and reloads the full sparse daily×service dict — unbounded cached blob
description: get_matrix serializes the entire cells dict as {f'{day}\x1f{svc}': v} into the cache, and on read rebuilds it by splitting every key. The cell count is days × distinct-services. For a 90-day window with hundreds of services this is tens of thousands of entries; closed windows are cached for 30 days, so many such blobs accumulate in SQLite. Every cache hit deserializes the whole dict even though downstream callers usually only need by_service() or total(). With many profiles/accounts/windows this multiplies into large persistent storage and per-request deserialization cost.
scenario: 5 profiles × 4 periods × an account with 300 services × 90 days = up to ~1.08M cell entries cached across keys, each round-tripped through dict<->JSON on every request. SQLite cache grows large and cold deserialization dominates request latency.
suggested_fix: Cache the already-reduced aggregates the routes need (by_service list and daily trend arrays) instead of the full sparse matrix, or store the matrix in a compact columnar form; consider not persisting full daily granularity for long closed windows when only service/trend rollups are consumed.

title: trend() aggregation is O(days × cells) — quadratic on wide daily windows
description: DailyServiceMatrix.trend() loops over each day in self.days and, inside, scans the entire self.cells dict filtering for that day: sum(v for (d,_s),v in self.cells.items() if d==day). That is O(len(days) × len(cells)) = O(days × days × services). For a 90-day window with 300 services, cells≈27,000 and days=90 → ~2.4M comparisons per trend render; for a 365-day window it is ~10x worse. by_service() is single-pass O(cells), so trend() is the outlier.
scenario: A 12-month daily trend (via a wide window) over an account with hundreds of services makes trend() scan the full cell dict once per day, turning a sub-second render into a multi-second CPU spin under load.
suggested_fix: Compute the trend in a single pass: iterate self.cells once accumulating into a {day: total} dict, then emit values in self.days order. O(cells) instead of O(days×cells).

title: Trend table/data endpoints ignore the configured cost basis (no pre_credit_gross spec)
description: api_trend_table (line 390) and api_trend_table_data (line 417) call ce.get_trend(window, granularity=gran) with NO spec, so get_trend falls back to console_default() = all record types (net after credits). Meanwhile api_trend_data (line 349), the summary cards, and the services tables all use spec=pre_credit_gross() (excludes Credit/Refund/Upfront). The same trend, rendered as a chart vs a table, therefore uses two different cost bases. On a credit-heavy or RI-upfront account the table totals will differ from the chart and from the summary card for the same period, exactly the 'numbers don't match' trust break the provenance design is meant to prevent. The cost_basis_label is also absent from these contexts so the user has no indication the basis changed.
scenario: Account with $50k of activation credits this quarter. The trend CHART (pre-credit gross) shows ~$50k higher monthly bars than the trend TABLE (net after credits) for the identical period and profile, with no label explaining the difference.
suggested_fix: Pass spec=pre_credit_gross() to get_trend in both api_trend_table and api_trend_table_data (matching api_trend_data and the summary/services routes), and include cost_basis_label in those contexts.

title: Closed-window classification uses end <= today, treating yesterday's still-finalizing data as immutable
description: _is_closed_window returns True when end <= dt.date.today() (UTC date from window.iso()). It then caches the matrix for 30 days with zero SWR (line 130). But CE data for very recent days is not final: AWS continues to restate the last ~24-72 hours (and month-end true-ups, tax, RI/SP allocations) for days after the usage date. A window ending exactly today/yesterday is classified 'closed' and frozen for 30 days, so late-arriving cost for the most recent day(s) never updates until the 30-day TTL expires. Also dt.date.today() is local-machine date while windows are UTC; if the server runs in a timezone behind UTC, 'today' can lag the window's UTC end and misclassify an open window as closed.
scenario: User views period='last_month' on the 1st of the new month. The window end == 1st-of-this-month <= today, so it's cached 30 days with no revalidation. AWS posts month-end RI/SP and tax true-ups for the prior month over the next few days, but the dashboard keeps serving the stale frozen total for up to 30 days.
suggested_fix: Only treat a window as truly closed when end is at least N days (e.g. 3) in the past to allow for CE restatement, and compute 'today' in UTC (datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()) to match the UTC windows; otherwise use the shorter open-window TTL/SWR.

title: Summary/services contexts are cached even when they contain an error
description: api_cost_summary and api_cost_services call cache_set(ckey, ctx) unconditionally, even when _build_*_ctx caught an exception and set ctx['error'] (with all numeric fields None/empty). Unlike the composition route which guards with `if ctx.get('error') is None` (line 332), these store the error context with the default TTL/SWR. A transient failure (throttling, expired creds, STS hiccup) thus gets cached, and subsequent requests return the cached error page for up to TTL+SWR even after the underlying issue clears.
scenario: CE briefly throttles (LimitExceeded) during the first summary load after deploy. The error ctx is cached for 30 min fresh + 6h stale; the dashboard keeps showing 'error' for hours despite CE recovering seconds later, until cache expiry or a manual bust.
suggested_fix: Guard cache_set with `if ctx.get('error') is None` in both api_cost_summary and api_cost_services (mirroring the composition route), or cache error results with a very short TTL.

title: CE call counter does not propagate into ThreadPoolExecutor worker threads; X-CE-Calls-Spent severely undercounts
description: CECountingMiddleware sets the `_current` ContextVar in the async dispatch, and FastAPI/anyio copies that context into the endpoint threadpool worker. But the actual CE calls in cost.py are dispatched into a *nested* `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)` (cost.py:59-66, 121-123) and into the SWR `_refresh_pool` (deps.py:99). A plain ThreadPoolExecutor does NOT copy contextvars into its worker threads (verified: a worker sees the ContextVar default, not the request value). Inside those workers, cost_explorer._get_cost_and_usage calls get_current_counter() which sees None and lazily creates a brand-new throwaway CECallCounter in the worker's own context (middleware.py:38-41). That throwaway is never merged back, so its calls/records are lost. The response counter the middleware reads only reflects CE calls made directly on the request thread (e.g. ce.get_forecast at cost.py:62 also runs in the pool, so it's lost too; ce.get_total_cost in resources_api runs on the request thread so it counts). Net effect: the X-CE-Calls-Spent and X-CE-Estimated-Cost-USD headers under-report by exactly the calls that go through the matrix/forecast/refresh pools — i.e. the majority of CE spend on the most-used pages.
scenario: Open /api/cost/summary?period=mtd on a cold cache. Three matrix fetches + one forecast all run in the nested pool, so each issues 1+ CE pages but the counter sees 0. The response reports X-CE-Calls-Spent: 0 (or only counts work done on the request thread) while AWS was actually billed for several CE requests. On large accounts with deep CE pagination (SERVICE x USAGE_TYPE over a 3-month daily window can paginate many times), the under-count grows with cardinality, so the cost-visibility dashboard misreports its own AWS bill the worst exactly when spend is highest.
suggested_fix: Capture the parent context and run pool tasks under it. Either pass the counter explicitly into CE calls, or wrap submissions with contextvars.copy_context(): e.g. `ctx = contextvars.copy_context(); pool.submit(ctx.run, fn, ...)`. For schedule_refresh, the refresh has no request context anyway, so explicitly attach a counter or accept that refreshes are uncounted — but document it. Centralize the wrapping so every pool.submit of a CE-touching callable inherits the request counter.

title: Per-thread CostExplorerClient dict is keyed by id(session) on freshly-created sessions → unbounded growth and id-reuse returning a wrong/dead client
description: get_ce_client caches clients per worker thread in `_ce_local.clients`, keyed by `id(session)`. But get_session (deps.py:106-112) constructs a NEW boto3.Session on every call and never caches it; every handler calls get_session at least once per request (often twice — once in the handler and again inside get_cost_source). So: (1) the dict grows by one entry per request per thread and is never evicted — unbounded memory growth, and each entry holds a live boto3 CE client (which itself caches endpoint/credential state), so this is a real leak proportional to request volume. (2) `id()` is only unique among *live* objects; once a request's transient Session is garbage-collected, CPython can reuse that address for a later Session. If the new Session's id() collides with a still-present dict entry, get_ce_client returns the OLD client (built for a different, now-dead session) — and worse, a different profile/account. That returns CE data for the wrong AWS account. The wrapper is also documented as not thread-safe, but a reused-id client could be handed to a different request on the same worker thread.
scenario: Run the dashboard for a while across multiple profiles. Memory climbs by ~one CE client per request on each Starlette worker thread; with thousands of requests the per-thread dict holds thousands of dead clients. Separately: request A (profile prod) builds Session S1, client cached at id(S1); S1 is GC'd after the request; request B (profile staging) builds Session S2 that happens to reuse S1's address; get_ce_client returns prod's CE client for the staging request, so staging's cost page silently shows prod's account data (or vice-versa). The 'account_id used as cache namespace' protection in cost_store does not help because the client itself is the wrong-account one.
suggested_fix: Do not key by id() of a transient object. Key the client cache by a stable identity (profile name / resolved account_id / credentials), and cache the boto3.Session itself by profile so the same Session object is reused. Bound the cache (e.g. LRU) so it cannot grow without limit. At minimum, hold a strong reference to the Session alongside the client so ids cannot be reused while the entry lives, and evict by profile.

title: Closed-window TTL classification uses local date (date.today()) against UTC window end → 30-day caching of a still-open day, or never-closing near midnight
description: _is_closed_window parses the window end (which is produced in UTC by core/time_windows.py) and compares `end <= dt.date.today()`. dt.date.today() returns the LOCAL date, not UTC. The windows themselves are explicitly UTC and use datetime.now(tz=utc). For any deployment whose local timezone is behind UTC (e.g. US timezones, where local date can be a day earlier than UTC for part of the day), a window ending 'today (UTC)' can be judged still-open when it is actually the current UTC day, or — more damaging — a window ending on the UTC boundary can be classified as CLOSED while UTC is still on that day, caching incomplete data for 30 days with swr=0 (no background refresh). For timezones ahead of UTC, the inverse: the current month/day stays mis-bucketed near the local/UTC date rollover.
scenario: Server in US/Pacific (UTC-7/8). At 18:00 local on the last day of a month, local date is still the last day but UTC has already rolled into the 1st. last_month()/current_month() produce a window ending at the UTC 1st-of-month. _is_closed_window sees end (UTC 1st) <= today (local last-day) is False for last_month edge cases, or for an mtd window ending 'now' the end date in UTC may equal a date already past locally, so a partial current period gets cached as closed (ttl=30 days, swr=0). The dashboard then shows a frozen, incomplete total for up to 30 days with no refresh path, on exactly the boundary days operators care about most.
suggested_fix: Compare against the UTC date, not local: use `dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).date()` (or compare the window end to a UTC 'now'). Since the entire windowing layer is UTC by design, the closed-window check must be UTC too.

title: cache_bust() with empty prefix does a full-table LIKE '%' scan/delete with no index; bust of large cache blocks all writers under the global lock
description: bust() runs `DELETE FROM cache_entries WHERE key LIKE ?` with `prefix + '%'`. The default call (export_api.py:204 `cache_bust()`) passes prefix='' → `LIKE '%'`, a full-table scan deleting every row. LIKE on the PRIMARY KEY text column is not sargable to a range scan in general (and certainly '%' matches all), so this is O(rows). It runs while holding the process-wide `self._lock`, and a large single DELETE transaction in WAL mode must write every deleted row to the WAL and then checkpoint. With a cache holding many large matrix/resource blobs (each entry can be a multi-MB JSON of a daily x service matrix or thousands of resource rows), the bust serializes behind the lock and stalls every other cache read/write (all of which open their own connections but the writers all contend on self._lock and on SQLite's single-writer). Even a prefix bust like 'matrix:' is a full scan because LIKE 'matrix:%' on a TEXT PK still scans unless the optimizer can use the PK range — and the broad default bust cannot.
scenario: An operator hits the 'clear cache' endpoint (export_api.py:204) on a long-running instance that has accumulated thousands of cache rows across many profiles/periods/regions, several of them multi-MB resource/matrix blobs. The single DELETE locks the cache; concurrently arriving dashboard requests that try to cache_set or read block on self._lock / SQLite writer for the duration, producing a visible stall. The cost grows with the number and size of cached blobs, i.e. exactly the large-account case.
suggested_fix: For full bust, use `DELETE FROM cache_entries` (or DROP/recreate / TRUNCATE-equivalent) instead of LIKE '%'. For prefix busts, rely on PK range bounds (`key >= prefix AND key < prefix||high_char`) so the PK index is used. Consider doing busts in batched deletes outside the global lock, or use a generation/epoch counter (bump an epoch, lazily ignore older entries) to make bust O(1).

title: New SQLite connection opened per cache call (connect + 2 PRAGMAs) — connection/PRAGMA churn and WAL contention under load and large payloads
description: _connect() opens a fresh sqlite3.Connection and runs `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` and `PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL` on EVERY get/set/get_swr/bust. journal_mode=WAL is a database-level, persistent setting; re-issuing it per call is wasteful, and setting journal_mode while other connections are mid-transaction can fail/return without switching. Every cache_get/cache_set in the hot path (every route in cost.py and resources_api wraps a cache_get + cache_set) pays connect + 2 pragma round-trips. Connections are also never explicitly closed — they rely on the `with` context manager which only commits, not closes (sqlite3 connection context manager does NOT close the connection), so connections leak until GC, leaving WAL readers open and delaying checkpoints. All writes serialize on a single process-wide self._lock, so concurrent writers (every page render caches its ctx) queue up; with timeout=5.0 a backlog of large writes (multi-MB matrix JSON) can exceed the busy timeout and raise OperationalError: database is locked.
scenario: Dozens of concurrent dashboard tabs across many profiles each render summary/services/resources, each doing cache_get then cache_set of a large ctx blob. Every call spins up a new connection and re-runs PRAGMAs; writes serialize on self._lock and SQLite's single writer. Under burst load with multi-MB resource/matrix payloads, set() calls back up past the 5s timeout and surface 'database is locked'. Leaked unclosed connections keep WAL from checkpointing, so the -wal file grows large.
suggested_fix: Use a single long-lived connection (or a small pool / thread-local connection) created once; set WAL/synchronous once at init. Always close connections explicitly (the with-block does not close them). Raise busy_timeout via PRAGMA and serialize only writes. Consider chunking/streaming or compressing very large blobs, or storing them outside SQLite.

title: Serializing very large matrices/resource lists to JSON in SQLite blows up memory and write cost; sparse-cell JSON encoding is O(days x services)
description: get_matrix serializes the entire daily x service matrix to a JSON dict with one entry per non-empty cell, key `f'{d}\x1f{s}'`, then cache_set json.dumps's it into a single TEXT column. For a 90-day DAILY window on an account with hundreds of services, cells approaches days*services (e.g. 90 * 400 = 36k cells), each a ~30-byte key plus a float — a multi-MB JSON string built fully in memory, written under the global write lock, and re-parsed (json.loads + a dict comprehension that splits every key on '\x1f' and re-tuples it, cost_store.py:120-123) on every cache hit. Resource ctx (resources_api build_resources_ctx) similarly caches thousands of resource dicts as one JSON blob. SqliteCache.get/get_swr load the full value_json and json.loads it whole even when the caller will filter/limit afterward (resources_api filters by service and limit AFTER loading the full cached list). This is the 'serialize huge lists to JSON in SQLite' hazard called out in scope.
scenario: A management account with hundreds of services over a 3-month daily trend, or an account with tens of thousands of EC2/EBS/S3 resources: the matrix/resource blob is many MB. Each cache_set holds the whole string in RAM and writes it under self._lock (stalling other writers); each cache hit json.loads the whole blob and rebuilds tuples even though the user only wants the top-50 by cost. Repeated across concurrent requests, peak memory and CPU scale with cardinality, defeating the point of the cache on the largest accounts.
suggested_fix: Store the matrix more compactly (e.g. per-day arrays aligned to a service index, or columnar) to cut key overhead and parse cost. For resource lists, cache already-trimmed/aggregated views or store rows in a queryable table so limit/service filtering happens in SQL, not after loading everything. Avoid rebuilding tuple keys on every read by storing in the consumed shape.

title: SWR refresh pool (max_workers=4) saturates across many keys; deduped-but-still-serialized refreshes starve and never-refresh hot keys
description: _refresh_pool has only 4 workers and is shared across ALL SWR keys (audit, resources, every profile/period/region combination). schedule_refresh dedupes per key, but each refresh producer (build_resources_ctx / build_audit_ctx) is itself heavy: it enumerates resources across all opted-in regions (N regions x describe calls) and/or runs a full audit, which can take many seconds to minutes on large accounts. With dozens of distinct (profile, region, period) keys going stale around the same time, at most 4 run concurrently and the rest queue unboundedly in the ThreadPoolExecutor's internal queue. Because each stale request only schedules (does not wait), users keep being served stale data while the queue backs up; a key whose refresh is stuck behind a slow region-wide enumerate may stay stale indefinitely, and the producer also creates fresh boto3 sessions/clients inside the pool thread (build_*_ctx calls get_session/get_ce_client), compounding the id(session) leak in get_ce_client on the refresh threads. There is also no timeout on the producer, so one hung describe/audit ties up a worker permanently, shrinking effective capacity below 4.
scenario: An org with 10 profiles x 30 opted-in regions browses the resources/audit pages; entries go stale after the SWR TTL. A wave of stale-hits schedules ~hundreds of refreshes, but only 4 run at once and each region-wide enumerate_all takes minutes. The queue grows without bound, refreshes for less-lucky keys never complete before they're scheduled again, and one region with a hung/throttled describe call permanently occupies a worker, leaving 3. Users see perpetually stale numbers and the process holds a growing backlog of pending heavy tasks.
suggested_fix: Bound and shed the refresh queue (e.g. drop schedule if pool is saturated, or use a bounded queue and reject), add a per-producer timeout, and consider separate pools or rate-limiting per profile. Reuse cached sessions/clients in producers. Track in-flight count and refuse to enqueue beyond a cap so a stale-storm cannot build an unbounded backlog.

title: get_swr lazy-delete opens a second connection under the lock for every expired read; expired-but-popular keys repeatedly DELETE
description: When age >= ttl+swr, get_swr opens a fresh connection AND acquires self._lock to DELETE the row (sqlite_cache.py:95-99). Reads otherwise take no lock, but every past-SWR read now contends for the global write lock and opens a second connection. For a key that is fully expired but still being polled (e.g. HTMX auto-refresh on a tab whose producer keeps failing so cache_set is never re-populated — note schedule_refresh only re-sets on success, deps.py:91), every poll re-runs the DELETE (the row is already gone after the first, so subsequent DELETEs match 0 rows but still take the lock and a connection). This adds avoidable write-lock contention to the read path under load.
scenario: A resources page whose background refresh keeps failing (e.g. throttled describe on a huge account, so build_resources_ctx raises and producer returns nothing) is polled every few seconds by many open tabs. Each poll past the SWR window grabs the write lock and opens a connection to delete an already-absent row, serializing against legitimate writers and adding churn precisely when the account is large/throttled.
suggested_fix: Skip the DELETE when the row is already known-expired/absent, or make lazy-delete best-effort without taking the global write lock (e.g. only delete occasionally, or rely on a periodic sweep). Returning (None, True) is enough for correctness; the physical delete can be deferred/batched.

title: Prewarm builds a CE client via get_ce_client on a transient session, seeding the leaking id(session) cache and running uncounted
description: prewarm_background loops over all profiles, each iteration calling get_session (a fresh, uncached Session) then get_ce_client(session). This seeds the per-thread id(session)-keyed client dict (deps.py:127) on the prewarm thread with one entry per profile, and those Session objects may be GC'd after the loop, leaving dead clients keyed by ids that can later be reused (same defect as the main get_ce_client finding, on the prewarm thread). The prewarm also issues an STS get_caller_identity plus the canonical matrix CE call per profile with no concurrency cap or inter-profile delay, so with many profiles it fans out serially but unbatched at startup. CE calls here also run outside any request context, so they are uncounted (acceptable, but means startup CE spend is invisible).
scenario: A deployment with ACU_ENABLE_PREWARM=1 and dozens of profiles starts up: prewarm makes dozens of STS + CE calls back-to-back and populates the prewarm thread's client dict with dozens of entries whose Sessions then become garbage, setting up id-reuse on that thread for any later work it does. On accounts where the mtd matrix paginates deeply (many services x daily granularity), each profile's prewarm is a multi-page CE fetch, multiplying startup CE spend invisibly.
suggested_fix: Reuse a cached session/client keyed by profile (fixing get_ce_client as above also fixes this). Optionally bound prewarm concurrency and add small backoff between profiles to avoid CE throttling at startup, and attach an explicit counter if startup CE spend should be tracked.

title: CE call counter undercounts: contextvar not propagated to ThreadPoolExecutor workers
description: The request-scoped CECallCounter is stored in a contextvars.ContextVar set by CECountingMiddleware. _build_summary_ctx (and _build_services_ctx at lines 121-123) submit the CE-calling work (src.get_matrix x3 and ce.get_forecast) to a plain concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor. ThreadPoolExecutor.submit does NOT copy the current context into worker threads (verified: a worker sees the ContextVar default). Inside those workers, cost_explorer._get_cost_and_usage and get_forecast call get_current_counter(), which finds _current.get() is None and fabricates a fresh throwaway CECallCounter. All pages/records counted there are written to that orphan object, never to the request's counter. The response headers X-CE-Calls-Spent / X-CE-Estimated-Cost-USD therefore systematically undercount: for the summary endpoint the 3-4 most expensive CE calls (the matrix fetches + forecast, each of which can be deeply paginated) are entirely invisible. The undercount worsens exactly when it matters most: a cold, large account where get_matrix paginates many pages of DAILY x SERVICE results across hundreds of services.
scenario: Cold-cache hit on /api/cost/summary for an account with hundreds of services and a 90-day daily window. get_matrix paginates dozens of pages in pool worker threads; the forecast adds another. The X-CE-Calls-Spent header reports 0 (only handler-thread direct calls count), so the operator's cost-of-querying estimate is wildly low, defeating the entire purpose of the counter.
suggested_fix: Capture the context at submit time and run work inside it. Either use a small wrapper: ctx = contextvars.copy_context(); pool.submit(ctx.run, src.get_matrix, ...), or pass the counter explicitly down into CostExplorerClient instead of fetching it from a ContextVar. Do the same in _build_services_ctx.

title: Throwaway counter leaks across requests in reused pool worker threads
description: get_current_counter() does c = _current.get(); if None it creates a CECallCounter AND calls _current.set(c). When this runs in a ThreadPoolExecutor worker thread (because the context was not propagated, see the cost.py finding), the set() mutates that worker thread's own thread-level context, which persists for the lifetime of the reused worker. The next, unrelated request whose work lands on the same pooled worker will find _current.get() returning the previous request's stale counter (verified: same object id accumulates across successive tasks on a reused single-worker pool). So pool-thread CE call/record counts from different requests and even different AWS profiles silently accumulate into one orphaned object that no one ever reads or resets. This is a per-thread cache leaking state across request boundaries.
scenario: Under sustained load the acu-refresh pool and the per-request ThreadPoolExecutors reuse a small fixed set of worker threads. Counter objects created on first use never get reset (only the middleware resets the handler-thread token), so a long-lived worker holds an ever-growing counter that conflates many requests/profiles. Combined with the propagation bug, debugging or any future attempt to read pool-thread counters yields cross-request-contaminated numbers.
